species.name: Arctic warbler
species.summary: A small leaf warbler that travels from northern breeding grounds to spend the non-breeding season in Southeast Asia.
species.identification: Dull brown-grey or olive upperparts, a long pale eyebrow, dirty-white underparts and one or two narrow wing bars. The lower bill has a dark tip.
species.diet: Small insects, spiders and other invertebrates picked from foliage.
species.activity: Feeds by day, mainly in the canopy and outer leaves.
species.behaviour: Moves actively through foliage and searches leaves and twigs for small prey.
species.reproduction: Breeds outside Singapore. It builds a domed nest on or close to the ground in northern scrub and tundra vegetation.
species.singapore: A very common migrant in Singapore forests, mangroves, parks and gardens. Its main chart period runs from about late September to early May. The Bird Society weekly chart uses eBird records from July 2016 through June 2026. The period is a guide, not a fixed annual schedule.
species.ecologicalRole: Consumes foliage-dwelling invertebrates and becomes part of Singapore forest food webs during migration.
species.pressures: Loss of wooded stopover habitat can reduce feeding and shelter options during its long journey.
species.habitat: Forest, Forest edge, Woodland, Mangroves, Parks, Gardens
species.rarity: Very common migrant; seasonal abundance and site use vary
species.fact: A dark tip on the lower bill helps separate it from the similar Two-barred warbler.

funFacts.text: A dark tip on the lower bill helps separate it from the similar Two-barred warbler.

funFacts.title: Canopy traveller
funFacts.text: It searches actively among leaves high in trees.

species.name: Asian brown flycatcher
species.summary: A small plain-coloured migrant that waits on a perch, then flies out to catch an insect.
species.identification: Plain ash-brown upperparts, whitish underparts and a broad pale base to the lower bill. Faint grey-brown marks can appear on the upper breast.
species.diet: Small flying insects and other invertebrates; some fruit may also be taken.
species.activity: Feeds by day from exposed or partly hidden perches.
species.behaviour: Uses short flights from a lookout perch to catch prey, then often returns to the same branch or a nearby perch.
species.reproduction: Breeds outside Singapore. It places a small cup nest in a tree cavity, broken trunk or other sheltered site in its breeding range.
species.singapore: A very common migrant in Singapore forests, parks, gardens, wooded areas and mangroves. Its main chart period runs from about late September to early April. The Bird Society weekly chart uses eBird records from July 2016 through June 2026. The period is a guide, not a fixed annual schedule.
species.ecologicalRole: Consumes insects in wooded habitats and links seasonal visitors to local food webs.
species.pressures: Removal of layered woodland and insect-rich resting habitat can reduce feeding cover during migration.
species.habitat: Forest, Parks, Gardens, Woodland, Mangroves
species.rarity: Very common migrant; seasonal abundance and site use vary
species.fact: An extensive pale base on the lower bill is a useful identification clue.

species.name: Barn swallow
species.summary: A fast aerial migrant with a deeply forked tail that sweeps over open areas for flying insects.
species.identification: Glossy blue-black upperparts, rufous forehead and throat, a complete dark breast band and a deeply forked tail. Adults can have long outer tail streamers.
species.diet: Flying insects caught in the air.
species.activity: Feeds by day in swift, sweeping flight and rests on wires or other open perches.
species.behaviour: Often feeds and roosts in groups. It changes direction quickly while hunting insects above land and water.
species.reproduction: Breeds outside Singapore. It builds an open cup from mud and plant material on sheltered ledges in its breeding range.
species.singapore: A very common migrant over Singapore wetlands, coasts, grasslands and other open ground. Its main chart period runs from about mid-September to late March. The Bird Society weekly chart uses eBird records from July 2016 through June 2026. The period is a guide, not a fixed annual schedule.
species.ecologicalRole: Consumes large numbers of flying insects and provides prey for larger birds.
species.pressures: Loss of insect-rich open habitat and disturbance at communal roosts can reduce safe feeding and resting space.
species.habitat: Open country, Wetlands, Coast, Grassland, Fields
species.rarity: Very common migrant; seasonal abundance and site use vary
species.fact: Its long, deeply forked tail helps separate it from the resident Pacific swallow.

funFacts.text: Its long, deeply forked tail helps separate it from the resident Pacific swallow.

funFacts.text: It catches flying insects without landing.

species.name: Besra
species.identification: Most Singapore records are of juveniles, which are most likely to be confused with Japanese Sparrowhawk and Shikra. Compared to juvenile Japanese Sparrowhawk, juvenile Besra has thicker dark undertail bands (visible when tail is spread), longer tail, more rounded wings, smaller head relative to body, and usually fewer primary bars. The yellow orbital ring and broader dark undertail bands separate it from juvenile Shikra. Adult plumages recall the Crested Goshawk, which is larger, shows six fingers in flight, and has more rounded wings. Male has cinnamon-rufous breast with a prominent dark mesial stripe; female is similar but is usually browner above.

species.fact: During the fall migration, this species is much less numerous than Shikra at the raptor migration watch point in Khao Dinsor in Thailand. In Singapore, while both species are very rare, Besra is much more commonly recorded than Shikra.

answers.label: A pointed beak and overlapping shell scutes distinguish typical hawksbills from green turtles. Keep a distance; do not handle a turtle to inspect its shell.

Most Singapore records are of juveniles, which are most likely to be confused with Japanese Sparrowhawk and Shikra. Compared to juvenile Japanese Sparrowhawk, juvenile Besra has thicker dark undertail bands (visible when tail is spread), longer tail, more rounded wings, smaller head relative to body, and usually fewer primary bars. The yellow orbital ring and broader dark undertail bands separate it from juvenile Shikra. Adult plumages recall the Crested Goshawk, which is larger, shows six fingers in flight, and has more rounded wings. Male has cinnamon-rufous breast with a prominent dark mesial stripe; female is similar but is usually browner above.
Look for mottled grey-brown fur, large eyes, curved claws and a broad membrane joining the limbs and tail. The folded membrane can be hard to see on a resting animal.

species.name: Booted Eagle
species.identification: A small crestless raptor with a long, square-cut tail and diagnostic pale shoulder spots ('headlights') on the upperwing; both morphs also show pale uppertail coverts. Dark morph has a uniform dark brown head and body, blackish flight feathers, and pale brown underwing coverts. Pale morph has mostly whitish underparts with fine brownish streaks, blackish flight feathers and whitish underwing coverts.

species.name: Brown shrike
species.summary: A masked migrant hunter that watches open ground from a clear perch.
species.identification: Brown upperparts, pale underparts, a dark eye mask and a pale eyebrow. Colour varies between the subspecies recorded in Singapore.
species.diet: Large insects, lizards, small birds and small mammals.
species.activity: Hunts by day from exposed perches in open habitats.
species.behaviour: Scans from a lookout, then drops or flies out to seize prey. It prefers more open ground than the Tiger shrike.
species.reproduction: Breeds outside Singapore. It builds an open cup nest in a shrub or small tree in its northern breeding range.
species.singapore: A common migrant in Singapore parks, grasslands and other open habitats. Its main chart period runs from about late September to late April. The Bird Society weekly chart uses eBird records from July 2016 through June 2026. The period is a guide, not a fixed annual schedule.
species.ecologicalRole: A small predator that links insects and small vertebrates to larger predators.
species.pressures: Loss of scrub edges and safe open feeding areas can reduce suitable migration habitat.
species.habitat: Parks, Grassland, Open country, Scrub
species.rarity: Common migrant; seasonal abundance and site use vary
species.fact: A dark stripe passes through each eye.

species.name: Chinese Sparrowhawk
species.identification: In all plumages, differs from other sparrowhawks by narrow pointed wings showing only four fingers in flight and nearly unmarked underwing-coverts. Adult male has uniform grey upperparts, red irides, dark grey orbital ring, orange-yellow cere, pinkish-orange breast, and obvious black wingtips. Female similar but with browner upperparts, yellow irides, and less uniform orange underparts. Juvenile has rufous-barred flanks and occasionally a mesial stripe, making them superficially similar to juvenile Grey-faced Buzzard, but that species has much longer and less pointed wings. Besra, Shikra, and Japanese Sparrowhawk have five fingers; Crested Goshawk and Eurasian Sparrowhawk have six.

species.name: Common Buzzard
species.identification: The Buteo buzzards present a stocky body and broad wings when in flight. Difficult to distinguish from Eastern Buzzard, but said to be darker brown overall, with dark carpal patch not contrasting with the rest of the wing as strongly. Can come in three distinct morphs: brown, rufous and dark. Brown morph with solid, brown wing lining and often possessing a pale breast 'belt' that separates the dark plumage of the belly from the strong upper breast streaking; tail also strongly barred. Rufous morph has dark brown underparts of brown morph replaced by warm rufous brown and less distinct tail barring. Dark morph has blackish-brown body plumage with pale flight feathers and a dark trailing edge to the wing. Crested Honey Buzzard shows a small protruding head and longer tail; Changeable Hawk-Eagle is larger with a prominent crest; Jerdon's Baza has a long crest and strongly barred underparts.

species.name: Common Kestrel
species.identification: Male has slaty-grey crown, nape, rump to uppertail, broad black subterminal tail-band, rufous rest of upperparts and wing-coverts with blackish markings, dark moustachial/cheek stripe and pale buffish underparts with dark streaks/spots on breast, belly and flanks. Female resembles male but has dark-streaked warm brown crown/nape and duller rufous upperparts with dark bars. Similar looking Lesser Kestrel is smaller, has yellow instead of black claws, proportionally longer central tail feathers, and proportionally shorter outermost primary (p10 shorter than p8 in Lesser Kestrel; while p10 is as long as p8 in Common Kestrel). Adult male Lesser Kestrels have less spotted upperparts and grey upperwing coverts and tertials.

species.name: Common redshank
species.summary: An active migrant wader with bright orange-red legs and a strong white wing pattern.
species.identification: Medium-sized with orange-red legs and a straight bill that is dark with red near the base. In flight, it shows broad white on the rear wing.
species.diet: Worms, insects, molluscs, crustaceans and other small wetland animals.
species.activity: Feeds by day and at night, often as tides expose feeding ground.
species.behaviour: Usually social and highly active while feeding. It runs after surface prey and also probes soft mud.
species.reproduction: Breeds outside Singapore. It makes a shallow ground nest hidden in wet grass in its breeding range.
species.singapore: A common migrant on Singapore mudflats, sandflats and brackish lagoons. Its main chart period runs from about early August to mid-April. The Bird Society weekly chart uses eBird records from July 2016 through June 2026. The period is a guide, not a fixed annual schedule.
species.ecologicalRole: Consumes coastal invertebrates and provides prey for larger wetland predators.
species.pressures: Loss and disturbance of intertidal feeding and roosting places can reduce safe refuelling habitat.
species.habitat: Mudflats, Sandflats, Brackish lagoons, Coast
species.rarity: Common migrant; seasonal abundance and site use vary
species.fact: Bright orange-red legs give this wader its English name.

funFacts.title: Red legs, clear clue
funFacts.text: Bright orange-red legs give this wader its English name.

funFacts.title: Day and night diner

species.name: Common sandpiper
species.summary: A small migrant shorebird that walks along water edges with a repeated tail-bobbing motion.
species.identification: Brown upperparts, clean white underparts, short greenish legs and a brown breast patch. In flight, look for a white wing bar and dark rump.
species.diet: Aquatic insects, worms, small crustaceans, molluscs and other invertebrates taken from wet surfaces and shallow water.
species.activity: Feeds by day and around suitable tidal conditions, usually along open water edges.
species.behaviour: Usually forages alone. It walks with a repeated tail bob and flies low with stiff, shallow wingbeats when disturbed.
species.reproduction: Breeds outside Singapore. It makes a shallow ground nest near freshwater in its northern breeding range.
species.singapore: A very common migrant across Singapore canals, ponds, reservoirs, mudflats and shores. Its main chart period runs from about early August to mid-April. The Bird Society weekly chart uses eBird records from July 2016 through June 2026. The period is a guide, not a fixed annual schedule.
species.ecologicalRole: Transfers energy from aquatic invertebrates to predators across freshwater and coastal food webs.
species.pressures: Disturbance and loss of quiet feeding edges can reduce the time available to rest and refuel during migration.
species.habitat: Canals, Reservoirs, Ponds, Mudflats, Coast, Mangroves
species.rarity: Very common migrant; seasonal abundance and site use vary
species.fact: It repeatedly moves its tail up and down while walking.

funFacts.title: The bobbing clue
funFacts.text: It repeatedly moves its tail up and down while walking.

funFacts.title: Check the rump
funFacts.text: Its rump looks dark in flight, unlike the white rump of the Green sandpiper.

species.name: Crested Honey Buzzard
species.occurrence: Very common migrant and uncommon visitor
species.identification: Has a small pigeon-like head, long slightly rectangular wings with six primary fingers, and long tail. Very variable plumage which ranges from white to rufous to black, with streaked or barred underside; upperparts brown to dark brown. For the migratory subspecies orientalis, male has dark reddish-brown iris and two thick dark tail bands; female has yellow iris and three thinner dark tail bands. The local torquatus race has a distinctive crest.
species.habitat: Woodland; anywhere in Singapore including urban areas during migration.
species.behaviour: One of the most common migrants in Singapore; often travels in large flocks. Raids bee and hornet hives for larvae, scanning from a perch before following insects to their nest.

species.name: Eastern Buzzard
species.identification: Stocky with round body, round wings, and proportionally short tail in flight. Adults darker than juveniles; juvenile shows pale underparts with brown breast band and dark carpal patches, while adult has darker, more uniform plumage, the wings and tail marked with diffuse, dark subterminal banding. Very difficult to distinguish from Common Buzzard; birds with paler underparts, more strongly contrasting carpal patch, and less well-defined black trailing edge are thought to be this species. Crested Honey Buzzard shows a small protruding head and longer tail; Changeable Hawk-Eagle is larger with a prominent crest; Jerdon's Baza has a long crest and strongly barred underparts.

species.name: Eastern Marsh Harrier
species.identification: Male generally white overall with a grey-black streaked head and upper breast, grey-black outer primaries, dark mantle, back, and lesser coverts. Female brown overall with streaked brown underparts, brown upperparts, streaked underwing coverts and pale barring on primaries. Immature is dark brown overall with white patches on face, white breast band and white streaked shoulders. Separated from Pied Harrier by more elongated head with gentler gradient of throat incline, broader and rounder wings, and more bulky body. Male separated from female Pied Harrier by cleaner underwing and grey/black hood (not brown). Female separated from female/immature Pied Harrier by fully streaked underparts. Immature separated from immature Pied Harrier by white on face and breast band.
species.habitat: Open country, reclaimed land, grasslands, and marshes; occasionally over woodland on passage.
species.behaviour: Surveys terrain using low, buoyant flight typical of harriers, with short flaps interspersed by glides. Often perches on or near the ground where it may be hidden from view.
species.fact: As suitable habitat is becoming more scarce in Singapore, wintering birds are not often encountered. This species may otherwise be seen at raptor-watch sites migrating over Singapore.

A pointed beak and overlapping shell scutes distinguish typical hawksbills from green turtles. Keep a distance; do not handle a turtle to inspect its shell.

Male generally white overall with a grey-black streaked head and upper breast, grey-black outer primaries, dark mantle, back, and lesser coverts. Female brown overall with streaked brown underparts, brown upperparts, streaked underwing coverts and pale barring on primaries. Immature is dark brown overall with white patches on face, white breast band and white streaked shoulders. Separated from Pied Harrier by more elongated head with gentler gradient of throat incline, broader and rounder wings, and more bulky body. Male separated from female Pied Harrier by cleaner underwing and grey/black hood (not brown). Female separated from female/immature Pied Harrier by fully streaked underparts. Immature separated from immature Pied Harrier by white on face and breast band.

species.name: Greater Spotted Eagle
species.identification: A large eagle with overall dark brown plumage, dark brown underwing coverts, slightly pale primaries and secondaries with dark wingtips, distinctive patch at the base of outer primaries, and a white vent. There is also a rare fulvescens morph which has a mostly buffish to rufous body and wing coverts, and contrasting black flight feathers and tail.
species.habitat: Open country.
species.behaviour: Takes carrion; also forages opportunistically over open ground.

species.name: Grey-faced Buzzard
species.identification: Adult has plain greyish-brown upperparts and upper breast, white throat with striking black mesial stripe, and rufous bars on belly and vent. Juvenile has browner upperparts, broad white supercilium, less prominent mesial stripe, and dark streaks on underparts. Long-winged appearance distinguishes it from sparrowhawks and Crested Goshawk.

species.name: Japanese Sparrowhawk
species.identification: Male has dark grey upperparts, pinkish-rufous barring on underparts, reddish eyes with yellow eyering, and yellow cere; mesial stripe faint or absent. Female about 15% larger, with browner upperparts, yellowish eyes, and grey-barred underparts. Juvenile has darker brown upperparts, white supercilium, streaked or spotted breast, and broken bars on flanks. In flight, shows five fingers and is broader-winged than Chinese Sparrowhawk (which has four fingers). Juveniles may be confused with juvenile Besra and juvenile Shikra, but those species have proportionally smaller heads, more rounded wings, and proportionally longer tail. Eurasian Sparrowhawk is larger, lacks mesial stripe, has six fingers, and a longer tail. Crested Goshawk differs by having six fingers, very prominent mesial stripe, and much more rounded wings.
species.habitat: Forest, forest edge, wooded areas and open country. In Singapore, may be observed anywhere during the migratory season.

species.name: Little egret
species.habitat: Rivers, canals, ponds and coastal wetlands
species.rarity: Common migrant; abundance varies with season and site
species.summary: A small white heron that feeds in shallow water. It uses both urban waterways and natural coastal wetlands.
species.identification: White plumage, a slender dark bill, dark legs and yellow feet in typical adults. Young birds can have greener legs.
species.diet: Small fish, crustaceans and insects. Fish and insects are prey here, not added catalogue groups.
species.activity: Often seen feeding in daylight; feeding opportunities depend on water levels.
species.behaviour: May disturb the water with its feet to reveal prey. It can feed with other egrets.
species.reproduction: Builds nests and lays eggs, often in colonies with other waterbirds. Both parents contribute to care. These species-level notes do not claim a local breeding colony.
species.singapore: A familiar migrant at Sungei Buloh and other wetlands, including pond and canal edges. NParks records it throughout the year, with higher numbers commonly between November and January.
species.ecologicalRole: A shallow-water predator that connects small aquatic animals to the wetland food web.
species.pressures: Wetland disturbance and loss can remove feeding and resting places. A locally common visitor still depends on suitable habitat elsewhere along its migration route.
species.watch: Watch from paths or hides. Avoid making birds fly away from feeding or resting areas, and never feed them.
species.fact: Its yellow feet can stir hidden prey from shallow water.

funFacts.title: Feet that find food
funFacts.text: A little egret can use its feet to stir prey from the water before striking.

funFacts.title: Seasonal head plumes
funFacts.text: Breeding plumage can include two narrow plumes behind the head.

species.name: Northern Boobook
species.identification: Has an overall dark brown coloration, large yellow eyes, small white patch above the bill, and whitish underparts with brown teardrop-shaped blotches. Separated from Brown Boobook by teardrop-shaped blotches on the underparts compared to rounder, heart-shaped blotches in Brown (heart-shaped markings in Northern may also be observed along the flanks). When in hand, Northern Boobook has a longer wing-to-tail ratio. Calls are diagnostic.
species.habitat: While on migration, will make use of any habitat with trees, including parks, gardens and scrubland. In comparison, Brown Boobook is rarely encountered outside of the central forests in Singapore.
species.behaviour: Hunts nocturnally from a perch, taking prey on the ground and in foliage. Rarely calls on migration.
species.fact: Hunts nocturnally from a perch, taking prey on the ground and in foliage. Rarely calls on migration.

species.name: Osprey
species.identification: Large raptor with dark brown upperparts, brown breast band, white underparts, and a thick dark eye-stripe. In flight, long slender wings are bent at the carpals into an "M" shape, with dark patches on the underwing near the carpal joints. Juvenile has white-fringed upperparts and buffish underwing coverts.
species.habitat: Coastal and freshwater areas; forages over open water.
species.behaviour: Almost exclusively fish-eating; plunges feet-first into the water to catch fish.
species.fact: The sole member of the family Pandionidae, reflecting its distinctiveness from all other raptors.

species.name: Pacific golden plover
species.summary: A long-distance migrant whose gold-spotted non-breeding plumage blends with mud, grass and shorelines.
species.identification: Non-breeding birds are brown with gold or buff spots above and pale buff underparts. Breeding birds have black underparts bordered by a broad white band.
species.diet: Insects, worms, molluscs, crustaceans and other small invertebrates found on open ground and shores.
species.activity: Feeds by day and around suitable tidal conditions.
species.behaviour: Often gathers in large flocks. Individuals run, stop and pick prey from the surface.

species.name: Peregrine Falcon
species.occurrence: Uncommon migrant and very rare resident
species.identification: The migratory subspecies calidus has slaty-grey upperparts, white or buffish underparts with dark bars, broad blackish moustachial streak and white ear coverts. Larger than Eurasian Hobby and Amur Falcon; the broad moustachial streak, barred underparts, broader wings, and bulkier build separate it from both. Juvenile has browner upperparts and underparts with dark streaks instead of bars. Subspecies ernesti is darker overall with a complete black hood, and sometimes has a strong orange suffusion on underparts.
species.habitat: Open country, secondary growth, farmland, mangroves and urban areas.
species.behaviour: While it typically nests on cliffs, it has adapted to tolerate high-rise buildings in cities. First confirmed local breeding record was in 2025, when a pair successfully nested on the OCBC Centre in the Central Business District.
species.fact: The Peregrine Falcon is considered to be among the fastest diving birds in the world and can reach a top speed exceeding 300 km/h when pursuing prey.

species.name: Pied Harrier
species.identification: Male is distinctive; overall white with all-black head, upper breast, median coverts and outer primaries, a large white patch on lesser coverts, and black outer primaries contrasting with whitish wings in flight. Female has a brown head with streaking to the breast, white thighs and vent, and extensive barring on primaries and secondaries, white 'shoulders' contrasting with brown lesser coverts, dark-tipped primaries, white uppertail coverts and dark bands on the uppertail. Immature resembles female but has brown head, underparts, upperwing and underwing coverts. Separated from Eastern Marsh Harrier by more rounded head with steeper gradient of throat incline, slightly narrower and more pointed wings, and more slender body. Female and immature separated from female Eastern Marsh Harrier by lack of streaking across whole underside, from immature Eastern Marsh Harrier by lack of whitish face and white band across the breast. Female separated from male Eastern Marsh Harrier by brown hood (not grey/black) and more extensive markings on the underwing.
species.habitat: Open country, reclaimed land, grasslands, and marshes.
species.behaviour: Surveys terrain using low, buoyant flight typical of harriers, with short flaps interspersed by glides. Often perches on or near the ground where it may be hidden from view.
species.fact: As suitable habitat is becoming more scarce in Singapore, wintering birds are not often encountered. This species may otherwise be seen at raptor-watch sites migrating over Singapore.

species.name: Pied Harrier
species.identification: Male is distinctive; overall white with all-black head, upper breast, median coverts and outer primaries, a large white patch on lesser coverts, and black outer primaries contrasting with whitish wings in flight. Female has a brown head with streaking to the breast, white thighs and vent, and extensive barring on primaries and secondaries, white 'shoulders' contrasting with brown lesser coverts, dark-tipped primaries, white uppertail coverts and dark bands on the uppertail. Immature resembles female but has brown head, underparts, upperwing and underwing coverts. Separated from Eastern Marsh Harrier by more rounded head with steeper gradient of throat incline, slightly narrower and more pointed wings, and more slender body. Female and immature separated from female Eastern Marsh Harrier by lack of streaking across whole underside, from immature Eastern Marsh Harrier by lack of whitish face and white band across the breast. Female separated from male Eastern Marsh Harrier by brown hood (not grey/black) and more extensive markings on the underwing.
species.habitat: Open country, reclaimed land, grasslands, and marshes.
species.behaviour: Surveys terrain using low, buoyant flight typical of harriers, with short flaps interspersed by glides. Often perches on or near the ground where it may be hidden from view.
species.fact: As suitable habitat is becoming more scarce in Singapore, wintering birds are not often encountered. This species may otherwise be seen at raptor-watch sites migrating over Singapore.

species.name: Yellow-rumped flycatcher
species.summary: A passage migrant that brings flashes of yellow and white to wooded Singapore habitats.
species.identification: Males have black upperparts, a broad white eyebrow and wing patch, plus a yellow rump and underparts. Females are grey-olive but keep the yellow rump and white wing marks.
species.diet: Mainly insects and other small invertebrates taken from foliage or caught during short flights.
species.activity: Feeds by day from canopy branches and lower lookout perches.
species.behaviour: Searches mainly in tree crowns but can use low perches in open woodland.
species.reproduction: Breeds outside Singapore. It uses a tree cavity or similar sheltered hole in its northern breeding range.
species.singapore: A common passage migrant in Singapore forests, parks, gardens and mangroves. Bird Society data show most records from late August to mid-November, with another passage in March and April. These periods are guides, not fixed annual dates.
species.ecologicalRole: Consumes insects in wooded habitats during its seasonal passage.
species.pressures: Loss of layered woodland and insect-rich stopover sites can reduce feeding and resting habitat.
species.habitat: Forest, Parks, Gardens, Woodland, Mangroves
species.rarity: Common migrant; seasonal abundance and site use vary
species.fact: Both sexes show a yellow rump, an important clue among similar flycatchers.

funFacts.title: A bright rear marker
funFacts.text: Both sexes show a yellow rump, an important clue among similar flycatchers.

funFacts.title: Two passage periods
funFacts.text: Most Singapore records occur during southbound and northbound migration periods.

species.statusNote: Singapore RDB3: Least Concern. “Native” means naturally occurring in Singapore and does not imply a breeding resident population.
species.globalStatus: Dated global assessment not verified in this edition
species.watch: Watch from paths or hides. Keep away from feeding and roosting groups. Do not flush birds for a photograph.

after.name: Arctic warbler
after.summary: A small leaf warbler that travels from northern breeding grounds to spend the non-breeding season in Southeast Asia.
after.identification: Dull brown-grey or olive upperparts, a long pale eyebrow, dirty-white underparts and one or two narrow wing bars. The lower bill has a dark tip.
after.diet: Small insects, spiders and other invertebrates picked from foliage.
after.activity: Feeds by day, mainly in the canopy and outer leaves.
after.behaviour: Moves actively through foliage and searches leaves and twigs for small prey.
after.reproduction: Breeds outside Singapore. It builds a domed nest on or close to the ground in northern scrub and tundra vegetation.
after.singapore: A very common migrant in Singapore forests, mangroves, parks and gardens. Its main chart period runs from about late September to early May. The Bird Society weekly chart uses eBird records from July 2016 through June 2026. The period is a guide, not a fixed annual schedule.
after.ecologicalRole: Consumes foliage-dwelling invertebrates and becomes part of Singapore forest food webs during migration.
after.pressures: Loss of wooded stopover habitat can reduce feeding and shelter options during its long journey.
after.habitat: Forest, Forest edge, Woodland, Mangroves, Parks, Gardens
after.rarity: Very common migrant; seasonal abundance and site use vary
after.fact: A dark tip on the lower bill helps separate it from the similar Two-barred warbler.

funFacts.title: A bill-tip clue
funFacts.text: A dark tip on the lower bill helps separate it from the similar Two-barred warbler.

funFacts.title: Canopy traveller
funFacts.text: It searches actively among leaves high in trees.

after.name: Asian brown flycatcher
after.summary: A small plain-coloured migrant that waits on a perch, then flies out to catch an insect.

before.name: Besra
before.identification: Most Singapore records are of juveniles, which are most likely to be confused with Japanese Sparrowhawk and Shikra. Compared to juvenile Japanese Sparrowhawk, juvenile Besra has thicker dark undertail bands (visible when tail is spread), longer tail, more rounded wings, smaller head relative to body, and usually fewer primary bars. The yellow orbital ring and broader dark undertail bands separate it from juvenile Shikra. Adult plumages recall the Crested Goshawk, which is larger, shows six fingers in flight, and has more rounded wings. Male has cinnamon-rufous breast with a prominent dark mesial stripe; female is similar but is usually browner above.

before.name: Chinese Sparrowhawk
before.identification: In all plumages, differs from other sparrowhawks by narrow pointed wings showing only four fingers in flight and nearly unmarked underwing-coverts. Adult male has uniform grey upperparts, red irides, dark grey orbital ring, orange-yellow cere, pinkish-orange breast, and obvious black wingtips. Female similar but with browner upperparts, yellow irides, and less uniform orange underparts. Juvenile has rufous-barred flanks and occasionally a mesial stripe, making them superficially similar to juvenile Grey-faced Buzzard, but that species has much longer and less pointed wings. Besra, Shikra, and Japanese Sparrowhawk have five fingers; Crested Goshawk and Eurasian Sparrowhawk have six.

before.name: Common Kestrel
before.identification: Male has slaty-grey crown, nape, rump to uppertail, broad black subterminal tail-band, rufous rest of upperparts and wing-coverts with blackish markings, dark moustachial/cheek stripe and pale buffish underparts with dark streaks/spots on breast, belly and flanks. Female resembles male but has dark-streaked warm brown crown/nape and duller rufous upperparts with dark bars. Similar looking Lesser Kestrel is smaller, has yellow instead of black claws, proportionally longer central tail feathers, and proportionally shorter outermost primary (p10 shorter than p8 in Lesser Kestrel; while p10 is as long as p8 in Common Kestrel). Adult male Lesser Kestrels have less spotted upperparts and grey upperwing coverts and tertials.

after.summary: An active migrant wader with bright orange-red legs and a strong white wing pattern.
after.identification: Medium-sized with orange-red legs and a straight bill that is dark with red near the base. In flight, it shows broad white on the rear wing.

after.activity: Feeds by day and at night, often as tides expose feeding ground.

after.reproduction: Breeds outside Singapore. It makes a shallow ground nest hidden in wet grass in its breeding range.
after.singapore: A common migrant on Singapore mudflats, sandflats and brackish lagoons. Its main chart period runs from about early August to mid-April. The Bird Society weekly chart uses eBird records from July 2016 through June 2026. The period is a guide, not a fixed annual schedule.
after.ecologicalRole: Consumes coastal invertebrates and provides prey for larger wetland predators.
after.pressures: Loss and disturbance of intertidal feeding and roosting places can reduce safe refuelling habitat.

after.rarity: Common migrant; seasonal abundance and site use vary

after.name: Common sandpiper
after.summary: A small migrant shorebird that walks along water edges with a repeated tail-bobbing motion.
after.identification: Brown upperparts, clean white underparts, short greenish legs and a brown breast patch. In flight, look for a white wing bar and dark rump.
after.diet: Aquatic insects, worms, small crustaceans, molluscs and other invertebrates taken from wet surfaces and shallow water.
after.activity: Feeds by day and around suitable tidal conditions, usually along open water edges.
after.behaviour: Usually forages alone. It walks with a repeated tail bob and flies low with stiff, shallow wingbeats when disturbed.
after.reproduction: Breeds outside Singapore. It makes a shallow ground nest near freshwater in its northern breeding range.

after.ecologicalRole: Transfers energy from aquatic invertebrates to predators across freshwater and coastal food webs.
after.pressures: Disturbance and loss of quiet feeding edges can reduce the time available to rest and refuel during migration.

before.name: Eastern Marsh Harrier
before.identification: Male generally white overall with a grey-black streaked head and upper breast, grey-black outer primaries, dark mantle, back, and lesser coverts. Female brown overall with streaked brown underparts, brown upperparts, streaked underwing coverts and pale barring on primaries. before.name: Japanese Sparrowhawk
before.identification: Male has dark grey upperparts, pinkish-rufous barring on underparts, reddish eyes with yellow eyering, and yellow cere; mesial stripe faint or absent. Female about 15% larger, with browner upperparts, yellowish eyes, and grey-barred underparts. Juvenile has darker brown upperparts, white supercilium, streaked or spotted breast, and broken bars on flanks. In flight, shows five fingers and is broader-winged than Chinese Sparrowhawk (which has four fingers). Juveniles may be confused with juvenile Besra and juvenile Shikra, but those species have proportionally smaller heads, more rounded wings, and proportionally longer tail. Eurasian Sparrowhawk is larger, lacks mesial stripe, has six fingers, and a longer tail. Crested Goshawk differs by having six fingers, very prominent mesial stripe, and much more rounded wings.

before.name: Little egret
before.habitat: Rivers, canals, ponds and coastal wetlands
before.rarity: Common migrant; abundance varies with season and site
before.summary: A small white heron that feeds in shallow water. It uses both urban waterways and natural coastal wetlands.
before.identification: White plumage, a slender dark bill, dark legs and yellow feet in typical adults. Young birds can have greener legs.
before.diet: Small fish, crustaceans and insects. Fish and insects are prey here, not added catalogue groups.
before.activity: Often seen feeding in daylight; feeding opportunities depend on water levels.
before.behaviour: May disturb the water with its feet to reveal prey. It can feed with other egrets.
before.reproduction: Builds nests and lays eggs, often in colonies with other waterbirds. Both parents contribute to care. These species-level notes do not claim a local breeding colony.
before.singapore: A familiar migrant at Sungei Buloh and other wetlands, including pond and canal edges. NParks records it throughout the year, with higher numbers commonly between November and January.
before.ecologicalRole: A shallow-water predator that connects small aquatic animals to the wetland food web.
before.pressures: Wetland disturbance and loss can remove feeding and resting places. A locally common visitor still depends on suitable habitat elsewhere along its migration route.
before.watch: Watch from paths or hides. Avoid making birds fly away from feeding or resting areas, and never feed them.
before.fact: Its yellow feet can stir hidden prey from shallow water.

Separated from Brown Boobook by teardrop-shaped blotches on the underparts compared to rounder, heart-shaped blotches in Brown (heart-shaped markings in Northern may also be observed along the flanks). before.name: Peregrine Falcon
before.occurrence: Uncommon migrant and very rare resident
before.identification: The migratory subspecies calidus has slaty-grey upperparts, white or buffish underparts with dark bars, broad blackish moustachial streak and white ear coverts. Larger than Eurasian Hobby and Amur Falcon; the broad moustachial streak, barred underparts, broader wings, and bulkier build separate it from both. Juvenile has browner upperparts and underparts with dark streaks instead of bars. Subspecies ernesti is darker overall with a complete black hood, and sometimes has a strong orange suffusion on underparts.
before.habitat: Open country, secondary growth, farmland, mangroves and urban areas.
before.behaviour: While it typically nests on cliffs, it has adapted to tolerate high-rise buildings in cities. First confirmed local breeding record was in 2025, when a pair successfully nested on the OCBC Centre in the Central Business District.
before.fact: The Peregrine Falcon is considered to be among the fastest diving birds in the world and can reach a top speed exceeding 300 km/h when pursuing prey.

before.name: Pied Harrier
before.identification: Male is distinctive; overall white with all-black head, upper breast, median coverts and outer primaries, a large white patch on lesser coverts, and black outer primaries contrasting with whitish wings in flight. Female has a brown head with streaking to the breast, white thighs and vent, and extensive barring on primaries and secondaries, white 'shoulders' contrasting with brown lesser coverts, dark-tipped primaries, white uppertail coverts and dark bands on the uppertail. Immature resembles female but has brown head, underparts, upperwing and underwing coverts. Separated from Eastern Marsh Harrier by more rounded head with steeper gradient of throat incline, slightly narrower and more pointed wings, and more slender body. Female and immature separated from female Eastern Marsh Harrier by lack of streaking across whole underside, from immature Eastern Marsh Harrier by lack of whitish face and white band across the breast. Female separated from male Eastern Marsh Harrier by brown hood (not grey/black) and more extensive markings on the underwing.
before.habitat: Open country, reclaimed land, grasslands, and marshes.
before.behaviour: Surveys terrain using low, buoyant flight typical of harriers, with short flaps interspersed by glides. Often perches on or near the ground where it may be hidden from view.
before.fact: As suitable habitat is becoming more scarce in Singapore, wintering birds are not often encountered. This species may otherwise be seen at raptor-watch sites migrating over Singapore.

funFacts.text: Adult has a slight crest, blackish head-sides and upperparts, whitish throat and upper breast with a rufous-chestnut underwing coverts and belly to vent. Juvenile has browner upperparts, whitish head-sides with dark eyestripe, and mostly whitish underparts and wing-coverts.

after.name: Yellow-rumped flycatcher
after.summary: A passage migrant that brings flashes of yellow and white to wooded Singapore habitats.
after.identification: Males have black upperparts, a broad white eyebrow and wing patch, plus a yellow rump and underparts. Females are grey-olive but keep the yellow rump and white wing marks.
after.diet: Mainly insects and other small invertebrates taken from foliage or caught during short flights.
after.activity: Feeds by day from canopy branches and lower lookout perches.
after.behaviour: Searches mainly in tree crowns but can use low perches in open woodland.
after.reproduction: Breeds outside Singapore. It uses a tree cavity or similar sheltered hole in its northern breeding range.
after.singapore: A common passage migrant in Singapore forests, parks, gardens and mangroves. Bird Society data show most records from late August to mid-November, with another passage in March and April. These periods are guides, not fixed annual dates.
after.ecologicalRole: Consumes insects in wooded habitats during its seasonal passage.
after.pressures: Loss of layered woodland and insect-rich stopover sites can reduce feeding and resting habitat.
after.habitat: Forest, Parks, Gardens, Woodland, Mangroves
after.rarity: Common migrant; seasonal abundance and site use vary
after.fact: Both sexes show a yellow rump, an important clue among similar flycatchers.

funFacts.title: A bright rear marker
funFacts.text: Both sexes show a yellow rump, an important clue among similar flycatchers.

funFacts.title: Two passage periods
funFacts.text: Most Singapore records occur during southbound and northbound migration periods.
